transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Yeah, um… I guess what brought me in is I don’t really feel like myself lately. The things I usually just do—like going on photography walks, helping mentor the kids, even keeping my calendar clean and organized—those used to kind of keep me grounded.

Now they just feel… flat. Heavy. Like I look at the camera bag and think about going out, and then I don’t. Same with the mentoring stuff, and I used to be the person people came to for organizing things—funny, because that’s basically my job too—but lately I just stop before I start. I’m not initiating things the way I normally would, and that’s what made me think maybe I should come in.
How long have you been feeling this way?

Um… I’d say about a year and three months, give or take. It sort of started after a family member’s health and behavior changed, and I ended up taking on more of the coordinating—appointments, calls, keeping track of things. Which, I mean, I’m usually good at that kind of thing, that’s my whole work life too, but somewhere in there it started feeling different. So… yeah, roughly fifteen months.
Do these changes feel mainly driven by the situation with your family member?

I’m not totally sure. I mean, it lines up with that, timing-wise, so part of me says yes, probably. But then I think… lots of people deal with family stuff and still manage to keep their routines, you know?

And it’s weird because organizing things is usually where I’m solid. Like at work, if someone needs a meeting moved or ten people coordinated, I can usually make that happen. I used to even color-code things—probably too much, honestly. My sister used to joke about it. So when it started feeling hard, I kind of blamed the family situation, but I don’t know if that explains all of it. It feels connected, but I can’t say it’s only that.
Have you felt this down or flat most days for the past two years?

Most days… yeah, I think flat is the better word than down. Like, not crying all the time or anything, but the stuff that normally makes me feel like me—going out with my camera, mentoring the kids, even just keeping my calendar neat—started feeling heavy.

I just stopped starting things, if that makes sense. I’d look at the camera bag and then somehow end up sorting old emails instead, which is not even useful, just… I don’t know. But two years? I’m not sure it’s been that long. It feels more like it’s been going on a long while, but I don’t think a full two years.
Before this past 15 months, have you ever had another period lasting at least two weeks when you felt similarly flat or lost interest in the things you usually enjoy?

Before this past year or so? I don’t think I had it like this, not for two weeks straight where it really stood out. I mean, I’ve had times where I got bored with things—like I’d buy a camera lens and then not use it for a while, which my friend used to tease me about because I’d research it for weeks and then it would just sit there—but that wasn’t the same.

This time it’s more like the things that usually make me feel like myself, like going on photography walks, mentoring the kids, even just keeping my calendar clean… they started feeling flat and heavy. And I just stopped initiating them. That’s really what made me come in.
Do you find yourself worrying excessively about a lot of different things?

I don’t know if I’d call it excessive. I mean, I worry about normal stuff—work things, whether I forgot to respond to someone, family things—but I’m not sure it’s “a lot of different things” in that way.

Sometimes I get stuck thinking about whether I handled something right, like if an email sounded too short. But then again, in my job, details kind of matter, so it’s hard to tell what’s worry and what’s just… being careful. What do you mean by excessive?
Do you find it hard to control the worrying once it starts?

Sometimes, I guess? It depends what it’s about. Like if it’s an email or a scheduling thing, I’ll replay it in my head, and then I’ll remember some completely separate thing, like whether I put the parking receipt in the right folder, which sounds ridiculous out loud.

But I don’t know if I’d say I can’t control it. Usually I can get pulled into something else if I have to. It’s more like my mind keeps circling back unless something interrupts me. Does that count as hard to control?
Over the past two weeks, have you felt sad or depressed most of the day nearly every day?

I don’t know if I’d say “sad” most of the day. Depressed is such a heavy word, you know? I have days where I feel kind of low or like I’m moving through wet cement, but then I’ll get distracted by something—like reorganizing a meeting agenda or noticing the office printer is doing that thing where it leaves a line down the page—and then I’m not really thinking about my mood.

So… nearly every day, most of the day? I’m not sure. I wouldn’t want to say yes if it’s not exactly that.
In the past two weeks, have you felt down, depressed, or hopeless?

I’m not sure. “Hopeless” feels like a really specific word, and I don’t know that I’d use that. Down, maybe here and there, but then I get pulled into whatever’s in front of me—like a calendar issue or somebody needing a document reformatted—and then I’m just dealing with that.

So… in the past two weeks, I guess I’ve had moments of feeling down, but I don’t know if it’s enough to say yes the way you mean it.
In the past two weeks, have you had much less interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?

Yeah… I think that’s actually part of why I came in. The things that usually make me feel like myself have just felt kind of flat lately.

Like, I usually like going out for photography walks—there’s this one street where the light hits the buildings in a really specific way around late afternoon, and I’ll take way too many pictures of the same fire escape, which sounds boring, but it’s calming for me. And mentoring the kids too, that usually matters to me. Even keeping my calendar clean, which I know is a weird thing to say I “enjoy,” but I do like when everything is organized.

Lately I just… don’t start those things. They feel heavy, like there’s no spark in them. I don’t know if it’s “much less pleasure” exactly, but yes, less interest, less pull toward doing them.
Do you often feel physically tense or unable to relax?

I don’t know if I’d say “often.” I mean, I get tense sometimes, sure, but then I’m also sitting at a desk a lot, and those office chairs—there’s one in the conference room that sinks down slowly while you’re sitting in it, which drives me crazy because then you’re suddenly lower than everyone else at the table.

But physically tense… I haven’t really been tracking it. Unable to relax, maybe sometimes, but I’m not sure if that’s what you mean. I guess I’d have to think about it more.
Over the past two weeks, have you been feeling unusually tired or low on energy?

I don’t know. “Unusually tired” is hard to judge because I feel like everyone at work is tired all the time, you know? The office has those fluorescent lights that make the afternoon feel longer than it is, and by the time I’m sorting emails or fixing someone’s travel itinerary for the third time, it’s like… of course I’m tired.

But over the past two weeks specifically? I haven’t really been measuring my energy. Some days I feel kind of drained, but I don’t know if it’s more than usual or just normal life catching up.
If the family situation had never happened, do you think you would still be feeling this same way?

I think… probably not the same way, no. It’s hard to separate it out because it’s been tangled up with that for a while now.

It started after my family member’s health and behavior changed, and then I kind of became the person coordinating things—calls, appointments, checking in, keeping track of who said what. It’s funny, at work I’m good at coordinating calendars and details, so everyone assumes that means I can just do it endlessly in my personal life too, like I’m a walking spreadsheet.

But yeah… this has been going on about a year and three months, I’d say. Since that shift happened. So if none of that had happened, I don’t know that I’d be feeling like this, at least not in this same way.
Has this been making it hard for you to function at work or take care of things you need to do day to day?

Some, yeah. Not like everything is falling apart. Work is mostly intact—I’m still getting the big things done, meetings still happen, people still get what they need. But I’ve noticed I miss little calendar details sometimes, or I’ll double-check something that used to be automatic, like whether I actually sent the attachment or put the right room number in.

And outside work, I’ve kind of pulled back. I used to do more photography outings, and I was mentoring a bit, but lately I don’t feel as present or reliable, so I’ve been saying no more than I used to. It’s not dramatic, but it’s there.
Do you feel your loss of interest and heaviness are mainly a reaction to the ongoing family situation?

Mostly, yeah, I think it’s tied to that ongoing family situation. But what made me actually come in wasn’t just “I’m stressed,” because everybody says that and then you feel silly bringing it up.

It was more like… the things that usually make me feel like myself started feeling flat and heavy. Like photography walks—I’d usually notice the light or a weird reflection in a window, and lately I just don’t even start. And mentoring the kids, too, I’ve pulled back from initiating that. Even keeping a clean calendar, which sounds boring, but that’s kind of my thing. When that started feeling like dragging furniture across carpet, I thought, okay, maybe this is more than just a bad week.
During this past year, have you often felt sad?

I don’t know if I’d say “sad” exactly, or at least not in a clean, obvious way. It’s more like… some days there’s this heaviness, and then other days I’m just going through the motions.

Sad is tricky, because when people say sad I picture crying at a movie or something clear-cut, and that’s not really how I’d describe it. I mean, I’ll be sitting at my desk looking at the calendar color-coding, and suddenly I’m thinking about how I used to care about making things neat, and then I end up reorganizing paper clips instead of answering the question in my own head. So… often? Maybe. I’m not totally sure.
When the family situation eases up, do you still feel this same flatness and loss of interest?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, when things calm down a little with family, I’ll expect myself to sort of snap back, like, okay, now go take the camera out or text the mentoring group or clean up the calendar tabs. But it still feels weirdly flat.

That’s actually why I came in. The stuff that normally feels like “me”—photography walks, helping with the kids, even keeping my calendar neat—started feeling heavy, like something I had to push myself toward, and then I just stopped starting those things. I can get distracted by all the family noise, sure, but even when it’s quieter, I’m not really reaching for those things the way I used to.
Over the past two weeks, have you been having trouble sleeping?

Yeah, some nights. Not every single night, but there have been nights where I only sleep maybe two or three hours and then I’m up before dawn.

And the weird part is I don’t always feel tired right away. I’ll wake up and my brain goes, okay, answer emails, update the appointment lists, fix that calendar thing—like it’s suddenly office hours at 4:30 in the morning. Which is ridiculous, because nobody needs an updated appointment list before sunrise, but there I am thinking about it.
When you sleep only two or three hours, do you still feel like you have plenty of energy the next day?

Yeah… sometimes, that’s the part that feels strange. If I only sleep two or three hours, I’ll wake up before dawn and instead of feeling wiped out, I’m like, okay, I can answer emails now, I can fix the appointment list, I can get ahead of things.

And then I’ll start thinking about whether the list should be sorted by date or by person, which is not really the point, but it feels important at the time. So yes, there are mornings where I feel like I’ve got enough energy, even though I barely slept.
During those times when you sleep only two or three hours and still have energy the next day, do you feel unusually energized?

Yeah, I guess “energized” is the word, but it’s not like fun energy. It’s more like I suddenly have to do everything at once.

I’ll start rebuilding work templates, then halfway through that I’m making care plans, then emailing relatives, then reorganizing files—like if I sit still for five minutes I’m somehow dropping the ball. And the files thing gets ridiculous because I’ll think, well, if the folders were named better then everything else would be easier, but then I’m in three different projects at once.

And outside work, I’ve kind of pulled back. I used to do more photography outings, and I was mentoring a bit, but lately I don’t feel as present or reliable, so I’ve been saying no more than I used to. It’s not dramatic, but it’s there.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the symptoms are still clearly tied to an identifiable stressor, which would favor adjustment disorder over major depressive disorder or generalized anxiety disorder.
doctor.question: Do you feel your loss of interest and heaviness are mainly a reaction to the ongoing family situation?

target_item.name: Negative_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: What made me come in is that the things that usually make me feel like myself—photography walks, mentoring the kids, even keeping a clean calendar—started feeling flat and heavy, and I just stopped initiating them.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the loss of interest and heaviness, which directly matches the diminished motivation, emotional engagement, and social interest described in this symptom item.

patient.answer:
Mostly, yeah, I think it’s tied to that ongoing family situation. But what made me actually come in wasn’t just “I’m stressed,” because everybody says that and then you feel silly bringing it up.

It was more like… the things that usually make me feel like myself started feeling flat and heavy. Like photography walks—I’d usually notice the light or a weird reflection in a window, and lately I just don’t even start. And mentoring the kids, too, I’ve pulled back from initiating that. Even keeping a clean calendar, which sounds boring, but that’s kind of my thing. When that started feeling like dragging furniture across carpet, I thought, okay, maybe this is more than just a bad week.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has had depressed mood, which would help distinguish major depressive disorder from adjustment disorder with depressed mood and generalized anxiety disorder.
doctor.question: During this past year, have you often felt sad?

target_item.reason: The question is asking specifically about feeling sad/depressed over the past year, but the provided symptom profile does not include a depressive mood/sadness item. The closest profile is Negative_Symptoms, but that focuses on diminished interest, motivation, and emotional expression rather than sadness itself.

patient.answer:
I don’t know if I’d say “sad” exactly, or at least not in a clean, obvious way. It’s more like… some days there’s this heaviness, and then other days I’m just going through the motions.

Sad is tricky, because when people say sad I picture crying at a movie or something clear-cut, and that’s not really how I’d describe it. I mean, I’ll be sitting at my desk looking at the calendar color-coding, and suddenly I’m thinking about how I used to care about making things neat, and then I end up reorganizing paper clips instead of answering the question in my own head. So… often? Maybe. I’m not totally sure.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the symptoms are persistent despite any breaks or changes in the family stressor, to distinguish adjustment disorder from a depressive disorder.
doctor.question: When the family situation eases up, do you still feel this same flatness and loss of interest?

target_item.name: Negative_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: What made me come in is that the things that usually make me feel like myself—photography walks, mentoring the kids, even keeping a clean calendar—started feeling flat and heavy, and I just stopped initiating them.
target_item.reason: The question is directly asking whether the flatness and loss of interest persist even when the family stress eases, which concerns diminished emotion, motivation, and interest.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think so. I mean, when things calm down a little with family, I’ll expect myself to sort of snap back, like, okay, now go take the camera out or text the mentoring group or clean up the calendar tabs. But it still feels weirdly flat.

That’s actually why I came in. The stuff that normally feels like “me”—photography walks, helping with the kids, even keeping my calendar neat—started feeling heavy, like something I had to push myself toward, and then I just stopped starting those things. I can get distracted by all the family noise, sure, but even when it’s quieter, I’m not really reaching for those things the way I used to.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has clinically significant insomnia, a key depressive symptom that would help distinguish major depressive disorder from adjustment disorder or generalized anxiety disorder.
doctor.question: Over the past two weeks, have you been having trouble sleeping?

target_item.name: Decreased_Sleep
target_item.manifestation: There have been nights when I sleep two or three hours, wake up before dawn, and feel ready to answer emails or update appointment lists instead of feeling tired.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question is directly about sleep trouble over the past two weeks, and the matching profile item concerns reduced sleep during elevated or driven periods.

patient.answer:
Yeah, some nights. Not every single night, but there have been nights where I only sleep maybe two or three hours and then I’m up before dawn.

And the weird part is I don’t always feel tired right away. I’ll wake up and my brain goes, okay, answer emails, update the appointment lists, fix that calendar thing—like it’s suddenly office hours at 4:30 in the morning. Which is ridiculous, because nobody needs an updated appointment list before sunrise, but there I am thinking about it.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the decreased need for sleep reflects an elevated or activated state suggestive of generalized anxiety rather than depression or adjustment disorder.
doctor.question: When you sleep only two or three hours, do you still feel like you have plenty of energy the next day?

target_item.name: Decreased_Sleep
target_item.manifestation: There have been nights when I sleep two or three hours, wake up before dawn, and feel ready to answer emails or update appointment lists instead of feeling tired.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether sleeping only two or three hours still leaves me feeling energized the next day, which directly matches decreased need for sleep.

patient.answer:
Yeah… sometimes, that’s the part that feels strange. If I only sleep two or three hours, I’ll wake up before dawn and instead of feeling wiped out, I’m like, okay, I can answer emails now, I can fix the appointment list, I can get ahead of things.

And then I’ll start thinking about whether the list should be sorted by date or by person, which is not really the point, but it feels important at the time. So yes, there are mornings where I feel like I’ve got enough energy, even though I barely slept.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the decreased need for sleep with preserved energy reflects a distinct hypomanic/manic episode, which would separate a mood episode from adjustment disorder, major depression, or generalized anxiety.
doctor.question: During those times when you sleep only two or three hours and still have energy the next day, do you feel unusually energized?

target_item.name: Increased_Activity
target_item.manifestation: During those stretches I start rebuilding work templates, making care plans, emailing relatives, and reorganizing files all at once, like sitting still would mean I’m dropping the ball.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the patient feels unusually energized during periods of little sleep, which most directly matches increased energy/activity.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I guess “energized” is the word, but it’s not like fun energy. It’s more like I suddenly have to do everything at once.

I’ll start rebuilding work templates, then halfway through that I’m making care plans, then emailing relatives, then reorganizing files—like if I sit still for five minutes I’m somehow dropping the ball. And the files thing gets ridiculous because I’ll think, well, if the folders were named better then everything else would be easier, but then I’m in three different projects at once.

inference.note: Added F31.8 due to decreased need for sleep with preserved energy and periods of increased goal-directed activity/multitasking, which raises concern for bipolar spectrum (hypomanic features). F41.1 is less supported given absence of clear excessive, hard-to-control worry across domains.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has a prolonged mood disturbance with reduced interest and functional decline, but also reports episodic decreased need for sleep (sleeping only 2–3 hours), preserved/heightened next-day energy, and periods of increased goal-directed, multitasking activity. These hypomanic-spectrum symptoms make a bipolar spectrum diagnosis more fitting than adjustment disorder or unipolar depressive episode, despite the psychosocial trigger.
